q: In which SDLC stage does the team meet users to find out and record exactly what the new system must do?
x: Requirements analysis gathers and documents what the users need the system to do. Design comes after it and decides how the system will do those things.

q: In which SDLC stage do programmers turn the approved design into working program code?
x: Writing the code from the design is the implementation (coding) stage. Planning and analysis come before any code exists; maintenance comes after the system is in use.

q: Six months after a school's fee system went live, the office reports a wrong total on one report and asks for a new SMS reminder feature. Which SDLC stage handles this work?
x: Fixing faults and adding small improvements to a system already in use is maintenance, the last SDLC stage. Requirements analysis is the early stage before the system was built.

q: Which order of these four SDLC stages is correct?
x: First decide what is needed, then design how to do it, then write the code, then test the code. Testing cannot come before implementation because there is no program to test yet.

q: Which statement best describes the Waterfall model?
o: Stages follow one after another, and each is finished before the next begins
The software is built in short cycles, each giving a working part to the client
Coding starts first and requirements are written after the program works
All stages run at the same time by separate teams
x: Waterfall is linear and sequential: each stage is completed before the next starts. Short cycles that each deliver a working part describe Agile, not Waterfall.

q: For which project is the Waterfall model the most suitable choice?
o: A payroll system whose rules are fixed by law and fully written down at the start
A new social app whose features will change with weekly user feedback
A game prototype where the client is unsure what they want
A startup's website that must show a working page to investors every two weeks
x: Waterfall works best when requirements are clear and stable from the start, as with fixed payroll rules. Changing or unclear requirements and frequent demos suit Agile.

q: What is a main weakness of the Waterfall model?
o: Changing requirements after a stage is finished is difficult and costly
Too little documentation is produced at each stage
The client sees working software after every short cycle
It has no separate testing stage
x: Because each stage is closed before the next begins, going back to change requirements means redoing later stages. Waterfall produces a lot of documentation and does have a testing stage.

q: Agile methods develop software by
o: completing all design before writing any code
writing full documentation before meeting the client
testing only once after the whole program is written
delivering small working parts in short repeated cycles
x: Agile is iterative and incremental: each short cycle (sprint) ends with a small working part. Finishing all design first is the Waterfall approach.

q: A team shows the client a working part of an app every two weeks, takes feedback, and changes its plan for the next two weeks. Which method is the team following?
o: A fixed-sequence plan with one review at the end
A requirements-first plan that allows no later changes
x: Short cycles with working software, regular client feedback and changing plans are the marks of Agile. Waterfall follows a fixed sequence and shows the client the product near the end.

q: Drawing flowcharts, planning the database tables and sketching screen layouts before any code is written belongs to which SDLC stage?
x: The design stage decides how the system will work: algorithms (flowcharts), data structure (tables) and interfaces (screens). Requirements analysis only records what is needed, not how to build it.

q: The finished system is installed at the client's office, old records are moved into it and staff are trained to use it. Which SDLC stage is this?
x: Installing the system, converting data and training users is deployment (some books call it installation). Testing happens before this, while the system is still with the developers.

q: During planning, a feasibility study is carried out to
o: find and fix errors in the finished program
train users after the system is installed
check whether the project is technically, financially and practically possible
x: A feasibility study decides early whether the project can and should be done: technology, cost and practicality. Finding and fixing errors belongs to testing and debugging, much later.

q: In project planning, a Gantt chart is used to show
o: the flow of control inside one program
the tables and keys of a database
tasks as bars against a timeline, with their start and end dates
x: A Gantt chart is a scheduling chart: each task is a bar placed along a time axis. The flow of control inside a program is shown by a flowchart.

q: While planning, a team notes that its only database expert might leave, so it arranges for a second member to learn the database work. This is an example of
x: Identifying something that could go wrong and planning a way to reduce its effect is risk management. No cost or dates are being worked out here.

q: A project needs 3 programmers for 4 months at Rs 100,000 per programmer per month, plus Rs 200,000 for software licences. What is the estimated cost?
x: Salaries: 3 × 4 × 100,000 = Rs 1,200,000; adding licences Rs 200,000 gives Rs 1,400,000. Rs 1,200,000 forgets the licence cost.

q: In a Waterfall plan the stages run one after another with no overlap: analysis 2 weeks, design 3 weeks, coding 5 weeks, testing 2 weeks. If analysis starts at the beginning of week 1, in which week does testing begin?
x: Analysis takes weeks 1-2, design weeks 3-5, coding weeks 6-10, so testing begins in week 11. Week 10 is the last week of coding (2 + 3 + 5 = 10 weeks used).

q: An Agile team works in 3-week sprints and gives the client a working increment at the end of each sprint. Sprint 1 starts at the beginning of week 1. At the end of which week does the client receive the 4th increment?
x: Sprints end at weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12, so the 4th increment arrives at the end of week 12 (4 × 3). Week 9 is the 3rd increment.

q: Which statement matches the Agile way of working?
o: The plan made at the start must be followed without change
The client is involved only at the start and the end
Working software is delivered only once, at the end
Changes in requirements are welcomed, even late in development
x: Agile values responding to change and frequent client involvement, so late requirement changes are accepted. A fixed plan and one final delivery describe the Waterfall style.

q: In software development, a design pattern is
o: a finished program that can be copied into any project
a chart showing the project's tasks against time
a list of test inputs and expected outputs
a general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring design problem
x: A design pattern is a proven template for solving a common design problem, adapted to each program. It is not ready-made code to copy; a chart of tasks against time is a Gantt chart.

q: A mistake in the requirements is noticed only during testing, not during analysis. Compared with catching it in analysis, fixing it now is usually
o: cheaper, because the code already exists to be edited
more costly, because design and code built on the mistake must also change
equally costly, because only the requirement document changes
free, because testing is meant to fix requirements
x: The later an error is found, the more work depends on it: the design and code made from the wrong requirement must be redone. That is why careful analysis early saves cost.

q: Which of these is NOT an activity of project planning?
o: Writing the source code for the login screen
Setting a timeline for each stage
Identifying risks and ways to reduce them
x: Planning covers cost, timelines and risks. Writing source code is implementation, done after planning and design.

q: Which statement about testing is true for the Waterfall model?
o: Testing is done inside every short cycle along with coding
Testing happens before the requirements are written
There is no testing; errors are fixed by users
The system is tested in its own stage after coding is complete
x: In Waterfall, testing is a separate stage that starts once implementation is finished. Testing inside every short cycle is how Agile works.

q: Compared with Waterfall, why does an Agile project usually show the client working software sooner?
o: Agile skips the testing of each part
Each short cycle ends with a small working part of the software
Agile writes all the code before any design
Agile needs no requirements from the client
x: Agile delivers a tested, working increment at the end of every short cycle, so the client sees software early. Agile still tests each part and still gathers requirements.

q: In software development, SDLC stands for
x: SDLC is the Software (or System) Development Life Cycle: the stages from planning to maintenance. The other expansions are not standard terms.

q: In a project timeline, a milestone is
o: the task that takes the longest time
the money set aside for unexpected costs
a key point that marks the completion of an important stage or deliverable
x: A milestone is a checkpoint, such as 'design approved', used to track progress. It marks an event, not a long task or an amount of money.

q: Project P: a bank's ATM software whose rules are fixed and must be fully documented at each stage. Project Q: a food-delivery app whose features will change as users react. Which choice of method fits both best?
x: Fixed requirements and full documentation at each stage suit Waterfall (P). Changing features driven by user feedback suit Agile (Q).

q: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for a result-checking app?
o: The app must show a student's marks when a roll number is entered
The result page must load within 2 seconds
The app must let the admin add a new subject
The app must print a mark sheet for a student
x: A non-functional requirement describes how well the system works, such as speed. Showing marks, adding subjects and printing mark sheets are things the system does, so they are functional requirements.

q: What is the main document produced at the end of requirements analysis?
o: A requirements specification listing what the system must do
A user's guide for the finished system
A list of bugs found during testing
x: Requirements analysis ends with a written requirements specification that design and testing later follow. Source code comes from implementation, and bug lists from testing.

q: In a strict Waterfall project, the client changes a requirement when coding is half done. What does the model require?
o: Ignore the change until the next sprint, two weeks later
Add the change directly in the code without updating any documents
Go back to update the requirements and design, then redo the affected later work
Stop testing, since requirements can no longer change
x: Waterfall stages build on the documents of earlier stages, so a change means returning to requirements and design and redoing what depends on them; this is why changes are costly. Sprints belong to Agile, and changing only the code leaves the documents wrong.

q: Risk exposure = probability × loss. Risk R1 has probability 0.5 and loss Rs 40,000. Risk R2 has probability 0.1 and loss Rs 300,000. Which statement is correct?
o: R1 has the higher exposure, Rs 20,000
R2 has the higher exposure, Rs 300,000
R2 has the higher exposure, Rs 30,000
Both have the same exposure, Rs 20,000
x: R1: 0.5 × 40,000 = Rs 20,000. R2: 0.1 × 300,000 = Rs 30,000, so R2 is higher. Rs 300,000 is R2's loss before multiplying by its probability.

q: A program that asks for two numbers and prints their quotient stops with an error when the user enters 0 as the second number. What kind of error is this?
x: The program compiled and started, and it fails only during execution for a particular input (dividing by zero), so it is a runtime error. A syntax error would stop the program from being translated at all, and a logic error gives a wrong result without stopping the program.

q: Which kind of error lets a program run to the end without any error message but gives wrong results?
x: A logic error is a mistake in the program's reasoning, such as a wrong formula; nothing stops the program, it just gives wrong output. Syntax and runtime errors produce error messages.

q: Following a program by hand, line by line, and writing down each variable's value after every step is called
x: A dry run is a manual trace of the code that helps find logic errors without a computer. Compiling translates the code; it does not trace values.

q:
What happens when this Python program runs?
```
total = 50
count = 0
print(total / count)
```
o: It stops with a runtime error (ZeroDivisionError)
It is rejected with a syntax error before running
x: The code is written correctly, but dividing by zero is impossible, so Python stops while running with ZeroDivisionError, a runtime error. There is no syntax mistake, so it is not a syntax error.

q:
What happens when this Python code runs?
```
marks = [45, 60, 72]
print(marks[3])
```
o: A runtime error (IndexError), because index 3 does not exist
A syntax error, because of the brackets
x: A list of 3 items has indexes 0, 1 and 2, so `marks[3]` fails while running with IndexError. 72 is `marks[2]`; counting from 1 is the usual slip.

q:
What kind of error does this Python code contain?
```
x = 7
if x > 5
    print("big")
```
o: Runtime error: x is not defined
Logic error: it prints the wrong word
Syntax error: the colon after the condition is missing
x: In Python an `if` line must end with a colon: `if x > 5:`. Without it the code breaks the language rules, so Python reports a SyntaxError; x is defined on the first line.
`/` is done before `+`, so b / 2 = 45 and 70 + 45 = 115, printed as 115.0. The code compiles and runs but the formula is wrong, a logic error; it should be `(a + b) / 2.0`.
With `i < 5` the loop adds i = 1, 2, 3, 4: sum = 10, and 5 is never added. The code is valid C, so this off-by-one mistake is a logic error; `i <= 5` would give 15.

`x = 5` is an assignment, not a comparison: x becomes 5 and the condition's value is 5, which is non-zero (true), so `five` is printed. Using `=` instead of `==` is a classic logic error; with `==` it would print `not five`.

q:
What is printed?
```
def is_even(n):
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return True
    return False

print(is_even(4), is_even(7))
```
x: 4 % 2 = 0, so the condition is false and the function returns False; 7 % 2 = 1, so it returns True. The output is `False True`: the function has a logic error, since it tests for odd numbers.

q:
This code should count the numbers that are 5 or more, but it prints 2. Which change fixes it?
```
nums = [3, 8, 5, 10]
count = 0
for n in nums:
    if n > 5:
        count = count + 1
print(count)
```
x: `n > 5` skips 5, so only 8 and 10 are counted (2). With `n >= 5`, 8, 5 and 10 are counted: 3. Using `count = n` would print 10, the last value above 5.

q: Sana tests only the `calc_tax()` function with several inputs before it is joined to the rest of the program. This is
x: Testing one function or module on its own is unit testing. Integration testing checks modules after they are joined together.

q: The login module and the results module each work correctly alone, but when combined, the results page cannot read the logged-in student's roll number. Which testing is meant to find this kind of fault?
o: A dry run of one function
x: Faults in how separate modules pass data to each other are found by integration testing, done after the modules are combined. Unit testing checks each module alone, where both worked.

q: A tester enters inputs and compares the outputs with the expected results without looking at the program's code. This is
x: Black-box testing checks behaviour from the outside: inputs and outputs only. White-box testing uses knowledge of the code inside.

q: A tester reads the code and chooses inputs so that both the `if` branch and the `else` branch of every decision run at least once. This is
x: Designing tests from the code's internal structure, such as covering every branch, is white-box testing. Black-box testing does not look at the code.

q: Before signing off, the client's own staff use the finished system for their real tasks to check that it meets the agreed requirements. This is
x: Acceptance testing is done by the client or users to decide whether to accept the system against its requirements. Unit and integration testing are done by the developers on parts of the system.

q: A function accepts ages from 18 to 60 inclusive and rejects all others. Which set of test values best checks the boundaries?
x: Boundary testing uses values on each limit and just outside it: 17 and 61 must be rejected, 18 and 60 accepted. The set 18, 30, 60 never tests a value just outside the range.

q: After fixing a bug in the fee calculation, the team re-runs all the earlier tests to make sure the fix has not broken anything else. This is
x: Re-running earlier tests after a change, to catch new faults caused by it, is regression testing. Beta testing gives the product to outside users.

q: While debugging, a programmer sets a breakpoint on a line. What does it do?
o: Pauses the program at that line so variable values can be examined
Deletes that line from the program
Makes the program skip that line every time
Ends the program with an error at that line
x: A breakpoint stops execution at the chosen line so the programmer can inspect variables and step through the code. The line itself is not removed or skipped.

q: Which statement correctly separates testing from debugging?
o: Testing fixes errors; debugging only reports them
Testing is done only by the compiler; debugging only by users
Testing shows that an error exists; debugging finds its cause and fixes it
They are the same activity with two names
x: Testing runs the program to reveal that something is wrong; debugging then locates the faulty code and corrects it. The roles are not reversed.
